terms.html: A short inpatient stay, usually under 24 hours, for a transient psychiatric crisis (often suicidal or homicidal ideation that resolves quickly) that does not require a full admission.

A California emergency involuntary detention for evaluation and treatment, lasting up to 72 hours, initiated by police or a designated clinician when a person, due to a mental health disorder (or, since SB 43, a severe substance use disorder), is a danger to self, a danger to others, or gravely disabled. See Grave disability, LPS conservatorship.

A California certification for up to 14 additional days of intensive involuntary treatment when a person remains dangerous or gravely disabled and will not accept voluntary treatment after a 5150 hold; the patient has the right to a certification review hearing and may request a writ of habeas corpus.
A California certification for up to 14 more days of intensive treatment specifically for a person who remains actively suicidal after a 5250 hold.

A California certification, available only in counties that have adopted it, for up to 30 additional days of treatment for a person who remains gravely disabled, often used while a conservatorship is being pursued.
A California court-ordered post-certification hold for up to 180 days for a person who remains dangerous to others.
The current U.S. national Suicide and Crisis Lifeline number (call or text), which replaced the older 1-800 crisis line number.

Albert Ellis's rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT) framework — Activating event, Belief, Consequences, Dispute, Effective new outlook — used to challenge irrational beliefs that drive emotional distress.

A disaster/crisis mnemonic — Arousal (calm the person with safety and comfort), Behavior (help the person function), Cognition (reality testing and accurate information) — used in the first hours after a traumatic event.

Albert Ellis's cognitive model stating that an Activating event does not directly cause emotional Consequences; an irrational Belief about the event does. Nursing use: dispute the irrational "should"/"must" belief rather than the event itself.

The MSE component testing the ability to interpret proverbs or metaphors ("People in glass houses shouldn't throw stones"); concrete, literal answers may indicate schizophrenia, intellectual disability, or brain dysfunction.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 11, p.389; Ch 7, p.213; Unit 2

terms.html: Use of alcohol or drugs to become intoxicated, or use of a prescription drug for a purpose other than the one it was prescribed for.
A therapeutic communication technique that shows nonjudgmental interest ("I follow what you said"); it does not mean agreeing, and it builds trust.
The process by which an underrepresented cultural group learns and adopts selected aspects of the dominant culture.
Drugs (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) that block the breakdown of acetylcholine; the mainstay pharmacologic treatment for Alzheimer disease.
Bluish discoloration of the hands and feet seen in starvation, from poor peripheral perfusion.
A defense mechanism in which a person expresses an unacceptable feeling through action instead of reflecting on it (a teen angry at parents starts staying out all night); mostly maladaptive.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 10, p.339; Syllabus p.131; Unit 3, 8

terms.html: Attending fully to a patient's content and meaning, interpreting both verbal and nonverbal cues, and responding with reflection or open-ended prompts; one of the first communication skills to use. Contrast: passive listening (sitting quietly while the patient rambles) is not therapeutic.
An intense, time-limited (usually under a month) biopsychosocial reaction to a threatening event, linked to the fight-or-flight response. Contrast: chronic stress.
A PTSD-like reaction (intrusion, avoidance, negative mood, arousal changes) that resolves within 1 month of the trauma; it can progress to PTSD if it persists beyond a month.
A person's capacity to survive and flourish after a stressor; affects physical health, psychological well-being, and social functioning.
Continued use of a substance (or a reward-seeking behavior, as in gambling disorder) despite ongoing adverse consequences.
A patient's ability to self-administer medications as prescribed; described as full, partial, or nil. Poor adherence is a leading cause of relapse in schizophrenia and mood disorders.

Significant emotional or behavioral symptoms that develop within 3 months of an identifiable stressor, are out of proportion to the stressor, and subside once the stressor resolves or a new level of adaptation is reached.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 19, p.732; Ch 29, p.1296; Unit 8

terms.html: Activities of daily living (bathing, toileting, dressing, transferring, eating) vs. instrumental ADLs (shopping, managing finances, using the telephone, transportation) that support independent living; IADLs are usually lost first in early dementia.

Legal documents (living will, durable power of attorney for health care) made while a person is competent, applied when the person becomes incapacitated; require two witnesses and notarization, not an attorney.

The outward, moment-to-moment expression of emotion, described by range (full/restricted), intensity (flat, blunted, increased), appropriateness, and stability (mobile/labile). Contrast: mood is the sustained internal emotional state the patient reports; affect is what the nurse observes.
Rapid, extreme shifts in mood with little provocation; a core diagnostic feature of borderline personality disorder.
Overt behavior intended to hurt, belittle, take revenge, or dominate another person; may be verbal or physical. Contrast: anger is the feeling; aggression is the behavior.
Failure to recognize or identify familiar objects, people, or sounds despite intact sensory (visual, auditory) function; seen in Alzheimer disease and other neurocognitive disorders.
A drug that binds a receptor and initiates the same response as the natural chemical messenger. Contrast: antagonist.

Marked fear or anxiety about two or more situations (public transportation, open or enclosed spaces, standing in a crowd or line, being outside the home alone) where escape might be difficult, leading to active avoidance.
A dangerously low circulating neutrophil (granulocyte) count, generally <500 cells/mm³, presenting with fever, sore throat, and mouth sores; the greatest risk is with clozapine.

A clinician-rated scale assessing tardive dyskinesia and other involuntary movements of the face, lips, jaw, tongue, trunk, and extremities, each scored 0 (none) to 4 (severe); done at baseline and at least every 3–6 months for any patient on an antipsychotic for more than 3 months.

An extrapyramidal side effect of antipsychotics causing subjective restlessness and an inability to sit still; frequently mistaken for anxiety or psychotic agitation, which can lead a provider to mistakenly increase the antipsychotic dose.

Increased heart rate and blood pressure, diaphoresis, anxiety, restlessness, and tremor that begin within about 12 hours of the last drink and can progress to seizures (usually within 48 hours) and delirium tremens.
The first 12-step, self-help fellowship for recovery from alcohol use disorder, based on peer support and a structured program of steps.
A personality trait marked by difficulty identifying and expressing one's own emotions, with concrete, externally oriented thinking; associated with somatic symptom disorder.

The dynamic regulatory process — involving the autonomic nervous system, HPA axis, cardiovascular, metabolic, and immune systems — by which the body actively adapts to maintain internal stability in the face of a stressor.

The cumulative "wear and tear" on the body and brain caused by chronic stress, reflected in abnormal biologic values (cortisol, blood pressure, metabolic markers); higher allostatic load predicts poorer physical and cognitive health and contributes to comorbidity and mortality in bipolar disorder.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 19, p.714; Ch 26, p.1078; Unit 7, 8

terms.html: Reduced fluency and productivity of thought and speech; a negative symptom of schizophrenia (also called poverty of speech).

A coping style in which a person meets their own needs by meeting others' needs (joining the Peace Corps after a breakup); generally a healthy, mature defense. Contrast with altruism as a Yalom curative factor below, which is the therapeutic benefit a group member gains from helping another member.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 10, p.339; Syllabus p.131; Unit 3, 8

terms.html: One of Yalom's 11 therapeutic factors in group psychotherapy — the self-esteem boost and reduced self-preoccupation a member gains from giving help to another member ("Helping him made me feel useful").
Holding two equally strong, opposing feelings at the same time, which makes decision-making impossible; common in schizophrenia.
Anorexia nervosa severity grading — mild ≥17, moderate 16–16.99, severe 15–15.99, extreme <15 kg/m².

A strong, uncomfortable emotional response to a provocation that feels incongruent with one's values or rights; adaptive when expressed assertively, maladaptive when too frequent, too intense, or expressed through explosive outbursts or chronic suppression (linked to heart disease).
Markedly diminished interest or ability to experience pleasure in activities that used to be enjoyable; a negative symptom of schizophrenia and a core symptom of major depressive episodes.

An eating disorder marked by significantly low body weight from restricted caloric intake, an intense fear of weight gain, and a disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced; subtypes are restricting type and binge-eating/purging type.

The neurologic/psychiatric lack of insight into one's own illness — not stubbornness or denial in the psychological sense, but a symptom of the disease itself (common in schizophrenia and dementia); drives medication nonadherence. The term itself is general knowledge; Boyd describes the phenomenon as "denial of illness" and "lack of insight."
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 24, p.916, 922, 952; general knowledge for the term; Unit 6

terms.html: A drug that binds a receptor and blocks the receptor's normal response to its natural chemical messenger. Contrast: agonist.

Toxicity from anticholinergic overdose or sensitivity, remembered by "hot as a hare, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, dry as a bone, red as a beet" (fever, mydriasis, delirium, dry mucous membranes, flushed skin); treated with physostigmine.

An uncomfortable feeling of apprehension or dread in response to an internal or external stimulus, with physical (tachycardia, tremor), emotional, cognitive, and behavioral components. Contrast: fear has an identifiable, external source; anxiety's source is often diffuse or anticipatory.
An alteration or loss of language ability (expressive, receptive, or both); common in neurocognitive disorders and stroke.
Complete inability to produce sound/speech; a classic conversion disorder symptom.
A gene variant that raises the risk of Alzheimer disease — about 3 times with one copy and 8–12 times with two copies.
Impaired ability to execute learned, purposeful motor movements (e.g., dressing, using utensils) despite intact motor strength and coordination.

Avoiding or restricting food intake because of a lack of interest in eating, sensory aversion to food characteristics, or fear of aversive consequences (choking, vomiting), without the body-image disturbance seen in anorexia nervosa.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 32, p.1488; detail general knowledge; Unit 15

terms.html: A nontherapeutic communication response ("Why did you do that?") that demands justification, feels accusatory, and often cannot be answered because the patient genuinely does not know why.
A legal tort — a threat or attempt to touch a person without consent that causes a reasonable fear of imminent harm; distinct from battery, which requires actual contact.

The deliberate, systematic, ongoing collection and interpretation of data about a patient's health, wellness, strengths, functional status, and actual or potential mental health problems; the first step of the nursing process.
A tendency for people with antisocial personality disorder and borderline personality disorder to pair up, which produces dramatic, chaotic relationships.
The process of gaining and keeping an interpersonal connection to a significant person; insecure attachment in early life is a leading explanation for antisocial personality disorder.
MSE components tested by serial 7s from 100, serial 3s from 20, or spelling "world" backward; the clinician chooses the task by the patient's education level.

Meets all diagnostic criteria for anorexia nervosa except that body weight is in or above the normal range despite significant weight loss; classified under OSFED (other specified feeding or eating disorder).
Adding a second medication to improve a partial response to the first (e.g., adding lithium to an antidepressant for treatment-resistant depression).
The ethical duty to respect a patient's right to self-determination and informed choice, such as a competent patient's decision to stop a medication.

Lack of interest or motivation in initiating and sustaining goal-directed behavior; a negative symptom of schizophrenia often mistaken for laziness, and the real barrier behind poor hygiene or missed appointments.

A legal tort — unpermitted physical contact with a person. Medical battery is treatment (including medication) given without informed consent or in violation of an advance directive; giving medication against a competent patient's will without legal authority exposes the nurse to liability.

Aaron Beck's theory that depression results from faulty information processing, producing automatic negative thoughts and cognitive distortions about the self, the world, and the future (the cognitive triad).

A biologic theory of bipolar disorder in which overreaction to reward cues drives manic symptoms (euphoria, decreased need for sleep), while deactivation of the same system drives depressive symptoms.

A nontherapeutic communication response that minimizes a patient's distress (Patient: "I have nothing to live for." Nurse: "Everybody gets down in the dumps."); dangerous because it can miss an actual suicide cue.
The ethical duty to do good and promote the patient's well-being, such as advocating for treatment that relieves suffering. Contrast: nonmaleficence (the duty never to intentionally harm).
The process of healing and learning to cope after a loss. Contrast: grief is the acute emotional reaction; bereavement is the longer process of adapting.

A normal reaction to significant loss (sadness, rumination, insomnia, poor appetite, weight loss) that can mimic a major depressive episode; clinical judgment distinguishes normal grief from a diagnosable depressive disorder.
Protein clumps, formed from abnormal cleavage of amyloid precursor protein, that destroy cholinergic neurons and disrupt synaptic connections; a hallmark pathology of Alzheimer disease.
Rapid, impulsive, uncontrollable eating of an unusually large amount of food in a discrete period (1–2 hours), typically followed by guilt or shame.
Recurrent binge eating with a subjective loss of control and marked distress, but without the compensatory behaviors (purging, fasting, excessive exercise) seen in bulimia nervosa.
An anorexia nervosa subtype with recurrent binge eating or purging behavior (self-induced vomiting; misuse of laxatives, diuretics, or enemas) within the last 3 months.
A holistic assessment and treatment model organized around three interdependent domains — biologic, psychological, and social — used to understand the whole patient.
Bipolar disorder defined by at least one full manic (or mixed) episode, typically also with depressive episodes; the classic "manic-depressive illness."
Bipolar disorder in which the person is mostly depressed with brief hypomanic (not fully manic) periods; often under-recognized because the elevated mood is less dramatic.
An impossible, illogical delusion not drawn from ordinary life experience — thought control, thought broadcasting, thought insertion, or thought withdrawal. Contrast: nonbizarre delusion.
See Boxed warning.
Viewing one's own body negatively and using it as the primary measure of self-worth; a risk factor for disordered eating.
Preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in physical appearance; historically grouped with somatoform disorders, now classified as an obsessive-compulsive–related disorder in DSM-5.
terms.source: Syllabus p.149; general knowledge for DSM-5 reclassification; Unit 12

terms.html: Seeing one's own body differently from how others actually see it — perceiving oneself as fat while objectively emaciated; central to anorexia nervosa.
Edward Hall's four zones of personal space — intimate, personal, social, public — whose size varies by culture; the nurse should ask permission before entering a patient's intimate zone.

The defining limits of an individual or a relationship — physical, psychological, and social — that keep a therapeutic relationship focused on the patient's needs; dynamic and must be actively maintained. Warning signs of boundary violations include gifts, secrets, extra unscheduled time, and feeling that only you understand the patient.
The FDA's strongest safety warning, printed in a bordered box in a drug's prescribing information, about a serious or life-threatening adverse reaction.

An 18-item clinician-rated scale measuring the severity of psychotic and general psychiatric symptoms over time, each item scored 1 (not present) to 7 (extremely severe); higher scores indicate worse symptoms.
A negotiated, nonjudgmental conversation to reduce risky substance use; SBIRT stands for Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment.

Recurrent binge eating plus compensatory behaviors (self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse, fasting, excessive exercise) occurring at least once a week for 3 months, with self-evaluation overly tied to body shape and weight, and little or no weight loss.

A bedside delirium screening tool: delirium is present when there is (1) acute onset and a fluctuating course and (2) inattention, plus either (3) disorganized thinking or (4) an altered level of consciousness.

A clinical judgment about a patient's ability to understand, appreciate, and reason about a specific decision at a specific time; made by the treatment team, not a court. Contrast: competency is a legal determination made by a judge.
terms.source: general knowledge for the clinical/legal distinction; Boyd 7e Ch 4, p.116–117; Unit 1

terms.html: Gerald Caplan's theory that a crisis is a problem that cannot be solved by a person's usual coping methods, producing disequilibrium with rising tension and anxiety; crises are time-limited (usually resolving in 4–6 weeks) and represent both danger and opportunity, since people are unusually open to learning new coping skills during one.
Actively identifying people at risk for suicide so that treatment can begin.

A collaborative process that assesses, plans, implements, coordinates, monitors, and evaluates services to meet an individual's health needs; the "broker model" links the patient to services and monitors their use.
Interpreting a mild bodily sensation as dangerous ("I'm having a heart attack"), which triggers or escalates a panic attack.
An overreaction or extreme anxiety response to an everyday situation once accumulated stressors exceed a cognitively impaired patient's coping threshold; common in dementia.
A psychomotor disturbance that includes stupor, mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, and repetitive behavior; may require treatment with lorazepam or ECT.
One of Yalom's 11 curative factors in group therapy — the open expression of affect (crying, venting) that purges or "cleanses" pent-up emotion and reduces tension.

A nontherapeutic communication response that directly disputes a patient's delusion or belief (Patient: "I'm a cowboy." Nurse: "If you are a cowboy, what are you doing in the hospital?"); arguing strengthens delusions rather than weakening them and lowers the patient's self-esteem.

A nontherapeutic communication response in which the nurse introduces an unrelated topic when a patient raises something difficult; usually reflects the nurse's own anxiety and teaches the patient that the original topic is off-limits.
Constant turmoil without resolution; distinguished from crisis because, by definition, "there is no such thing as a chronic crisis" — a true crisis is time-limited.

A medication used to restrict a patient's behavior or movement that is not part of standard treatment for the patient's condition, or is given at a dose above the standard therapeutic dose for that purpose. See Restraint.
Vomiting, sweating, and nightmares that occur after an anticholinergic medication is stopped abruptly; a reason to taper rather than stop anticholinergics suddenly.
An ongoing physiologic stress reaction that causes cumulative wear and tear on the body; adaptive acute stress responses become maladaptive when prolonged. Contrast: acute stress.

A biologic theory of bipolar disorder in which sleep deprivation and disruption of circadian/social rhythms can precipitate manic episodes, and seasonal light changes can trigger winter depression or summer hypomania.
Speech loaded with excessive, often irrelevant detail that eventually reaches the point; common in obsessional thinking and in schizophrenia (where it is usually called circumstantiality).
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 28, p.1218; Ch 24, p.924; Unit 6, 9

terms.html: Extremely detailed, lengthy discourse that eventually reaches the intended point, unlike tangentiality, which never returns to the point. Contrast: tangentiality.
The 10-item Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised; scores range 0–67, and a score under 10 usually requires no additional medication for withdrawal.
Words strung together based on their sound rather than their meaning ("right, light, sight, might"); seen in mania and schizophrenia.

Ivan Pavlov's model of learning in which a neutral stimulus, repeatedly paired with a stimulus that naturally produces a response, comes to produce that response on its own (a bell paired with food eventually causes salivation by itself); the theoretical basis for systematic desensitization and exposure therapy for phobias.
The iterative nursing decision process of observing and assessing data, identifying the prioritized patient concern, and generating evidence-based solutions.
A therapy group in which all members begin together and no new members are admitted once it starts; typical of outpatient, sequential-curriculum, or psychotherapy groups. Contrast: open group.
Odd or eccentric personality disorders — paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal.
Dramatic, emotional, or erratic personality disorders — antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic.
Anxious or fearful personality disorders — avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive.
A toxic, longer-acting metabolite formed in the liver when cocaine and alcohol are used together; increases cardiotoxicity.

A relationship pattern in which a person close to someone with a substance use disorder inadvertently reinforces the substance use, often by covering for or protecting the user. Closely related to enabling.

The system of interrelated mental abilities — perception, reasoning, judgment, memory, intuition — that allow awareness of self and surroundings; impairment of cognition can prevent a person from recognizing their own illness.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 13, p.522; Ch 39, p.1875; Unit 4, 11

terms.html: A highly structured psychotherapy that alters distorted beliefs and maladaptive behaviors by identifying and replacing negative, inaccurate automatic thoughts and by changing the reinforcement of behaviors.

Automatic "twisted thinking" patterns generated from inaccurate interpretation of information — overgeneralization, personalizing, catastrophizing, selective abstraction — that maintain depression and anxiety.

Enduring patterns of thought that filter, code, and evaluate incoming information, allowing in only what matches one's existing picture of self and world; maladaptive schemata cause the misreading of others typical of personality disorders.
A depressed person's negative automatic thoughts about three domains — oneself, the world, and the future.

The ability of a group to stick together, especially important in task groups; a "double-edged sword" because very cohesive groups can also transgress healthy boundaries. Contrast: groupthink, which looks similar but means avoiding conflict rather than genuine connection.
Two facilitators sharing responsibility for leading a group; effective only when both coleaders attend every session and plan together before and after.
An evidence-based screening tool for the severity and intensity of suicidal ideation, suicidal behavior, and lethality; can be used in person, by phone, or by telehealth.
An auditory hallucination that instructs the person to act, ranging from innocuous to dangerous; always assess what the voices are telling the patient to do, especially toward self or others.
A signed agreement in which a patient commits to engaging in treatment and using emergency services if suicidal; has replaced the ineffective "no-suicide contract."

Responses, or unnecessary topic changes, that inhibit therapeutic communication — advice, agreement, challenging, false reassurance, disapproval. See Nontherapeutic Communication Techniques for the full list with examples.
Patterns within a group showing who is most liked, who holds power, which subgroups have formed, and who is isolated.
A defense mechanism in which a person makes up for a real or perceived weakness by excelling in a different area (a student who is poor at sports becomes a top debater).

A legal determination, made by a court, of a person's ability to understand and appreciate information at a specific time in order to consent to or refuse treatment; it is decision-specific and can change over time. A person's choice does not have to be rational to be competent. Contrast: capacity.

A trauma syndrome following chronic, repetitive trauma (especially betrayal of trust) that includes core PTSD symptoms plus affective dysregulation, a persistent negative self-concept, and relational problems; recognized in ICD-11 but not a separate diagnosis in DSM-5.
Being stuck in chronic mourning with intense yearning for the deceased for more than 6 months; affects an estimated 10%–20% of bereaved people.
Affirmations in solution-focused brief therapy that reinforce a patient's past successes and the strengths that produced them, creating hope for change.
Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in a ritualistic way to prevent or relieve the anxiety caused by an obsession.
Lack of abstraction; an inability to interpret proverbs or metaphors beyond their literal meaning; common in schizophrenia.
Making up a plausible but imagined account of events to cover a gap in memory, without intent to deceive; classic in Korsakoff amnestic syndrome and seen in other neurocognitive disorders.

The professional's ethical and legal duty not to disclose patient information shared in the course of care. Contrast: privacy. See Legal & Ethical entries for HIPAA and the exceptions to confidentiality.

A therapeutic communication technique that points out inconsistencies between a patient's thoughts, feelings, and actions ("I was in the room yesterday when you refused to speak with him"); used cautiously, nonjudgmentally, and only within a trusting relationship.

A court-ordered arrangement appointing a substitute decision-maker (conservator) for a person found unable to manage personal care or finances. A probate conservatorship is used for people with dementia or other incapacity; an LPS conservatorship is used specifically for grave disability from mental illness. See LPS conservatorship.
Recurrent concerns a patient expresses in different ways across multiple sessions (for example, repeated references to loss).
The integrated system of settings, services, clinicians, and levels of care that spans from acute illness to wellness.
The act of unconsciously transforming psychological distress into a physical symptom (sudden "paralysis" of the arm before a feared confrontation).

Severe emotional distress or unconscious conflict expressed through neurologic symptoms (paralysis, aphonia, blindness, seizure-like episodes) that do not match a recognized neurologic disease and have negative diagnostic tests. See La belle indifférence.
A deliberate, planned psychological effort to manage demands that are appraised as stressful.

terms.term: Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia (CSDD)
names: Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia
terms.html: The best-validated depression screening scale for patients with dementia; uses information from both the patient and an informant.
Dementia resulting from a disease process that globally affects the cerebral cortex, such as Alzheimer disease. Contrast: subcortical dementia.

The nurse's or provider's own emotional reaction to a patient, based on the clinician's unconscious needs and past relationships; the clinician's job is to recognize it through supervision and self-reflection so it does not erode professional boundaries. Contrast: transference.

An 11-item scale (pulse, sweating, restlessness, pupil size, bone/joint aches, rhinorrhea/tearing, GI upset, tremor, yawning, anxiety/irritability, gooseflesh) used to grade opioid withdrawal severity: 5–12 mild, 13–24 moderate, 25–36 moderately severe, >36 severe; buprenorphine induction is often started once withdrawal reaches the moderate range.
terms.source: general knowledge; Boyd 7e Table 31.4, p.1441; Unit 13

terms.html: An intense urge or desire to drink or use a substance despite knowing the negative consequences.

A time-limited event (adaptation usually occurs within 4–6 weeks) in which a person's usual coping fails to meet a perceived challenge or threat, with adaptive or nonadaptive outcomes possible; it is both a danger and an opportunity, since people are unusually open to learning new coping skills during a crisis. Types include developmental (maturational), situational, and traumatic (adventitious/social). Contrast: chaos is not a crisis because it has no resolution.
Specialized, short-term, goal-directed therapy for acute distress, typically lasting under 6 hours, aimed at stabilization and preventing hospitalization.
A community program pairing mental health specialists with specially trained police officers as first responders to manage mental health crises and divert people from jail into treatment.
A level of care, usually lasting less than 7 days, used when a crisis does not resolve quickly; the goal is symptom control rather than full treatment.
Behavioral techniques used in eating disorder treatment that change either the environmental trigger (cue) for disordered eating or the behavioral response to it.
Actively bridging and mediating messages and beliefs between a patient's cultural group and the health care system.

A set of academic and interpersonal skills that allow a clinician to be respectful of, and responsive to, a patient's health beliefs, practices, and linguistic needs. Contrast: cultural humility, a more recent concept emphasizing lifelong self-reflection rather than mastery of a fixed skill set.
A lifelong process of critical self-reflection used to continually readdress the power imbalance in the clinician-patient relationship; recommended as a strategy to combat implicit bias.
terms.source: Lecture: Implicit Bias and Mental Health Stigma; Unit 1

terms.term: Cultural syndrome / idiom of distress / cultural explanation
terms.html: DSM-5's replacement terms for the older, now-discouraged term "culture-bound syndrome": a symptom cluster recognized within one culture (ataque de nervios), a culture's characteristic way of talking about distress (susto, nervios), and a culturally specific explanation for symptoms, respectively.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 2, p.76–77; Ch 3, p.91; Unit 1

terms.html: The recurring phases of intimate partner violence — tension building, acute battering, and the "honeymoon" phase of remorse and reconciliation — that increase in frequency and severity over time.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 23, p.879–880; Syllabus p.183; Unit 10

terms.html: A chronic mood disorder with numerous periods of hypomanic symptoms alternating with numerous periods of depressive symptoms, less severe than bipolar I or II, present for at least 2 years.

A CYP450 inhibitor slows the metabolism of another drug and raises its blood level; a CYP450 inducer speeds up metabolism and lowers the level (for example, cigarette smoking induces CYP1A2, lowering levels of some antipsychotics).

"Talking the person down" through authentic engagement, respect, a calm demeanor, offering choices, and giving physical space; the preferred intervention before medication or seclusion/restraint when a patient is escalating.
Reconstruction of a traumatic event by the survivor, usually in a group format after a disaster; not compulsory and not recommended for everyone, since it can retraumatize some survivors.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 21, p.818; Ch 29, p.1274; Unit 10

terms.html: A nontherapeutic communication response that protects a third party instead of hearing the patient's concern ("Your doctor is very good; she wouldn't do that."); it dismisses the patient's complaint rather than exploring it.

Conscious or unconscious coping styles that protect the ego against anxiety; everyone uses them, and they become maladaptive when their persistent, rigid use interferes with functioning. See the full list of individual mechanisms (Acting out, Altruism, Compensation, Conversion, Denial, Devaluation, Displacement, Dissociation, Fixation, Humor, Idealization, Identification/introjection, Intellectualization, Isolation of affect, Passive aggression, Projection, Projective identification, Rationalization, Reaction formation, Regression, Repression, Splitting, Sublimation, Substitution, Suppression, Undoing) alphabetized under their own letters. Memory hook: suppression is conscious; repression is unconscious.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 10, p.338–343; Ch 27, p.1134; Syllabus p.131; Unit 3, 8

terms.html: The mid-20th-century policy of releasing long-confined psychiatric patients into the community for treatment, support, and rehabilitation; spurred by the 1963 Community Mental Health Centers Act and widely considered a failure by the 1990s because community services were never adequately funded. Contrast: institutionalization.

An acute disturbance of consciousness and cognition that develops over hours to days, caused by a medical condition, a substance, or multiple etiologies; usually reversible with treatment of the underlying cause, and always a medical emergency. Contrast: dementia, which develops gradually and is usually not reversible.
The most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, marked by autonomic hyperarousal, disorientation, and hallucinations; typically occurs 48–72 hours after the last drink and is a medical emergency.

A fixed, false belief that is not changed by reasonable argument or evidence, even when it contradicts the person's culture or education; types include grandiose, nihilistic, persecutory, and somatic. Contrast: hallucination (a false sensory perception) and illusion (a misperception of a real stimulus).

A chronic, usually progressive cognitive impairment, classified by its underlying cause (Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal) rather than by symptom pattern; may be cortical or subcortical. Contrast: delirium.

A defense mechanism in which a person refuses to acknowledge a painful reality (a teen whose best friend moves away insists he isn't sad; a patient having an MI insists it's indigestion); can also describe a substance user's inability to accept loss of control over use.

A general term for the body's physiologic (and often psychological) adaptation to continued substance or medication use, such that stopping abruptly produces a withdrawal syndrome. Contrast: tolerance (needing more of the substance for the same effect) and addiction/substance use disorder (continued use despite harm, with impaired control) — a person can be physiologically dependent on a prescribed medication without having an addiction. See Physiologic dependence, Tolerance, Withdrawal.
An experience of one's self as strange, unreal, or detached from one's own mental processes or body. Contrast: derealization.
Persistent or recurrent feelings of detachment from one's own mental processes or from one's surroundings, with intact reality testing (the person knows the feeling isn't real).

A common mental state of sadness, loss of interest or pleasure, guilt or low self-worth, disturbed sleep or appetite, low energy, and poor concentration; the core feature of major depressive disorder.
A feeling that one's surroundings are unreal, dreamlike, or distorted. Contrast: depersonalization.
The process of safely withdrawing a person from an addictive substance, usually under medical supervision, to manage withdrawal symptoms.

A defense mechanism in which exaggerated negative qualities are attributed to oneself or another person (a rejected boyfriend is suddenly "stupid and ugly"); common in borderline personality disorder alongside idealization.
A crisis tied to a predictable life transition, such as leaving home, finishing school, or taking on adult responsibility; based on Erikson's developmental stages.

A cognitive-behavioral therapy (developed by Marsha Linehan for borderline personality disorder) that combines behavior change strategies with acceptance-based (Zen) practice; teaches skills in emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness, distress tolerance, and mindfulness.
A model in which a genetic or biologic predisposition (diathesis) combines with environmental stress to trigger the onset or worsening of a mental disorder.
Judging people and events into mutually exclusive, extreme categories — all good or all bad — with no middle ground; related to splitting.
Self-imposed restrictive eating "rules" that, paradoxically, set off the next binge; the behavioral link between dieting and binge eating.
An innate temperament profile marked by withdrawal from new stimuli, low adaptability, and intense emotional reactions, often with aggression, inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity.
A group leadership style in which the leader controls interaction by giving directions and information and allowing little member discussion. Contrast: indirect leadership.
A nontherapeutic communication response that judges a patient's behavior ("You should be. How could anyone kill their mother?"); patients learn to avoid a nurse who disapproves of them.
A sudden, overwhelming event causing great damage and suffering that exceeds a community's own resources and requires outside help.
Acting on thoughts, impulses, or feelings without the social judgment that normally restrains them; a frontal-lobe symptom common in frontotemporal dementia and advanced Alzheimer disease.
A defense mechanism in which feelings about one person or situation are shifted onto a safer, less threatening target (a person argues with their boss, then comes home and yells at the children).

A childhood diagnosis for severe irritability and temper outbursts that begin before age 10 and are far more frequent or severe than developmentally expected; created in DSM-5 specifically to prevent overdiagnosing pediatric bipolar disorder.

A disruption in the normal links among a person's awareness, feelings, thoughts, behavior, and memories, so that the person feels detached or "disappears" and observes events from a distance; can be a normal brief coping response ("spacing out") or, when severe, a dissociative disorder.
Inability to recall important, usually stressful, personal information that is too extensive to be explained by ordinary forgetting.

Sudden, unexpected travel away from home with an inability to recall one's past, confusion about identity, or assumption of a new identity; in DSM-5, a specifier of dissociative amnesia rather than its own diagnosis.
terms.source: Syllabus p.150; general knowledge for DSM-5 status; Unit 12

terms.html: The presence of at least two distinct personality or identity states that recurrently take control of a person's behavior, with gaps in recall between them; formerly called multiple personality disorder.
Impaired ability to think abstractly, plan, initiate, sequence, monitor, and stop complex behavior; a core domain of neurocognitive disorder.
Receptor subsensitivity that develops from decreased cellular response to continued stimulation, such as with chronic antidepressant or antipsychotic use.
An intense physical and emotional pursuit of a lower body weight that overrides normal body cues such as hunger; a core psychological feature of anorexia nervosa.

The American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual, which organizes mental disorders by symptom patterns, with subtypes and specifiers, rather than by lab tests; DSM-5-TR (2022) dropped the multiaxial system used in DSM-IV-TR. See Five-axis system.
A model of grief describing oscillation between loss-oriented coping (confronting the loss directly) and restoration-oriented coping (taking a break to attend to life's ongoing demands).

terms.term: Duty to warn / duty to protect
terms.html: The legal obligation, established by Tarasoff v. Regents, for a mental health clinician to exercise reasonable care to protect an identifiable, foreseeable victim of a patient's threatened violence, which overrides ordinary confidentiality. See Tarasoff v. Regents.
A group of exactly two people; the smallest possible interpersonal group. Contrast: triad (a group of three).

A sudden, involuntary muscle spasm causing abnormal posturing (neck twisted, eyes rolled upward); usually the first extrapyramidal symptom to appear, often within hours to days of starting an antipsychotic; treated emergently with IM benztropine or diphenhydramine.
The Eating Attitudes Test (a 26-item self-report screening tool; a score above 20 warrants follow-up) and the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire, a more detailed clinical assessment tool.

The DSM-5 category that includes pica, rumination disorder, avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, and other specified/unspecified feeding or eating disorders.
Parrot-like, involuntary repetition of another person's words or phrases; seen in catatonia and some neurocognitive disorders.
Involuntary imitation of another person's movements; often accompanies echolalia in catatonia.
Feeling "high," "ecstatic," or "on top of the world"; a mild form of euphoria seen in hypomania and mania.

A brief electrical current that induces a generalized seizure (25–150 seconds) under general anesthesia and a muscle relaxant; its exact mechanism of antidepressant action is unknown, but it is highly effective for severe, treatment-resistant, or psychotic depression and for catatonia.
A coping strategy that reduces stress by reinterpreting the meaning of a situation rather than changing the situation itself. Contrast: problem-focused coping.

Difficulty accepting and managing one's own emotions in social interactions — mood instability, sudden mood "crashes," rejection sensitivity, and intense anger; a core feature of borderline personality disorder, and in eating disorders, disordered eating itself is often used to regulate overwhelming emotion.
The direct, almost contagious transmission of feelings — especially anxiety — from a patient to the nurse; notice when your own speech speeds up around an anxious patient.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 10, p.335; Ch 7, p.223; Unit 3

terms.html: Imagining and understanding another person's feelings and communicating that understanding back to them, without taking on the feeling as one's own. Contrast: sympathy, which is expressing one's own compassion or pity rather than understanding the other's experience; empathy is the therapeutic goal.

A therapeutic communication technique that invites a patient to describe their subjective experience in detail ("What does the voice seem to be saying?"); essential when assessing hallucinations, since command hallucinations are a safety risk that must be identified.
A therapeutic communication technique that invites the patient to judge the outcome of their own experience ("How did that work out for you?"), building self-reflection and ownership of change.

terms.term: Encouraging formulation of a plan of action
names: Encouraging formulation of a plan of action
terms.html: A therapeutic communication technique that helps a patient build concrete coping and problem-solving skills ("What could you do to let your anger out harmlessly?").
A family pattern of extreme emotional intensity with weak interpersonal boundaries and low individual autonomy; associated with eating disorders.

Erik Erikson's eight-stage lifespan theory, each stage built around a central conflict to resolve, with a successful outcome if resolved well: infancy, trust vs. mistrust (drive and hope); toddlerhood, autonomy vs. shame and doubt (self-control and willpower); preschool, initiative vs. guilt (direction and purpose); school age, industry vs. inferiority (method and competence); adolescence, identity vs. role diffusion/confusion (devotion and fidelity); young adulthood, intimacy vs. isolation (affiliation and love); adulthood, generativity vs. stagnation (production and care); and maturity/older adulthood, ego integrity vs. despair (renunciation and wisdom). Nursing use: assess whether a patient's developmental tasks were met and set age-appropriate goals.
The study of how culture and genetic differences among population groups influence medication response, metabolism, and side effects.
Exaggerated, unrealistic feelings of well-being; a symptom of mania.
Stress produced by a positive event (a wedding, a promotion) that is still physiologically activating. Contrast: distress, stress from a negative event.
A normal, neither elevated nor depressed, mood. Contrast: euphoric (elated), dysphoric (depressed, disquieted, restless), labile (rapidly changeable).

A lifelong problem-solving approach that integrates the best available research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient preferences and values; the first step is always defining the clinical question.
Solution-focused brief therapy questions that identify times when a problem was absent or less distressing, so those exceptions can be amplified and repeated.
One of Yalom's 11 group therapy curative factors — confronting the ultimate concerns of existence: death, isolation, freedom, and meaninglessness.
A lack of restraint in expressing feelings, often paired with an inflated, overvalued sense of self-importance and indiscriminate enthusiasm; a feature of mania.
A therapeutic communication technique that examines an idea or feeling in greater depth ("Tell me about it." "What happens when you feel anxious?").
The first-line behavioral therapy for OCD — exposing the patient to a feared trigger while preventing the compulsive ritual, to demonstrate that anxiety decreases on its own without the ritual.
Repeated real or simulated exposure to a feared object or situation until desensitization occurs; the treatment of choice for specific phobias.
Acute, drug-induced abnormal movements — dystonia, pseudoparkinsonism, akathisia — caused by dopamine (D2) blockade in the basal ganglia, most often from first-generation antipsychotics.

Intentional production or feigning of physical or psychological symptoms, motivated solely by the psychological desire to occupy the sick role (not for an external benefit); formerly called Münchausen syndrome. Contrast: malingering, which has an external motive.

A person (usually a caregiver, often a mother) deliberately causes or fabricates illness in another person (usually a child) to gain attention and sympathy from health care providers; a severe form of child abuse requiring mandated reporting. Formerly called factitious disorder by proxy / Münchausen by proxy.
A legal tort — holding a competent, voluntary patient against their will without a legal basis, such as refusing a voluntary patient's discharge request.
A nontherapeutic communication response offering empty comfort that may not be true ("Hang in there. Everything will turn out just fine."); it blocks the patient from exploring their actual feelings.
A family's participation in, or adjustment of routines to, a member's OCD rituals (for example, repeatedly providing reassurance); reducing family accommodation improves treatment outcomes.
A syndrome of disordered eating, menstrual dysfunction (amenorrhea), and osteoporosis seen in female athletes under pressure to maintain a low body weight.

Metabolism of an orally administered drug in the GI wall and liver before it reaches systemic circulation, which reduces the amount of active drug available. Related: bioavailability, the percentage of an administered dose that reaches circulation unchanged.

The older multiaxial diagnostic framework — Axis I (clinical disorders), Axis II (personality disorders and intellectual disability), Axis III (general medical conditions), Axis IV (psychosocial/environmental problems), Axis V (Global Assessment of Functioning) — dropped in DSM-5 in favor of nonaxial documentation and ICD Z-codes for psychosocial factors. See Global Assessment of Functioning.
terms.source: Syllabus p.27; general knowledge for DSM-IV-TR origin; Unit 2

terms.html: A defense mechanism in which development never progresses beyond an immature stage (an adult who still has tantrums when frustrated).
Absence of observable emotional expression. Contrast: blunted affect, in which emotional expression is present but greatly diminished.
Illogical, rapid connections between quickly changing thoughts, so the listener struggles to keep up; a hallmark of mania.
A behavioral technique in which the feared object or situation is presented repeatedly, without breaks, until the person's anxiety dissipates on its own.
A therapeutic communication technique that keeps a scattered conversation centered on one topic ("This point seems worth looking at more closely.").
The two officially designated roles in any group — leader and member. Contrast: informal group roles.
A mnemonic for the elements of a brief substance use intervention — Feedback, Responsibility, Advice, Menu (of options), Empathy, Self-efficacy.

Sigmund Freud's psychoanalytic theory describing personality as composed of the id, ego, and superego (see Id, ego, superego), with anxiety functioning as a danger signal and defense mechanisms protecting the ego against it; also proposed a series of psychosexual developmental stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital).
A patient's ability to carry out personal care, home management, work or school responsibilities, and social roles.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 11, p.398; Ch 18, p.686; Unit 2

terms.html: A 7-item self-report screening tool for generalized anxiety disorder severity, scored 0–3 per item (total 0–21): 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–21 severe; a score ≥10 is a commonly used referral cutoff.
A non-substance behavioral addictive disorder with tolerance (needing larger bets for the same excitement), withdrawal-like irritability when unable to gamble, and "chasing losses."

Hans Selye's model of the body's nonspecific physiologic response to any stressor, in three stages: alarm (fight-or-flight activation), resistance (the body adapts and copes), and exhaustion (resources are depleted and illness develops if stress continues). Chronic corticosteroid secretion during stress contributes to illness.
The MSE component assessing a patient's appearance (dress, hygiene, fit for the weather), psychomotor activity, eye contact, and overall behavior.
Excessive, difficult-to-control worry and apprehension about multiple real-life matters, present for at least 6 months, accompanied by somatic symptoms such as muscle tension and fatigue.
A yes/no depression screening tool designed for older adults; the 15-item short form is scored 0–15.
A late-life developmental shift from a materialistic, rational view of the world to a more cosmic one, with growth in spirituality and a positive use of solitude.

A nontherapeutic communication response in which the nurse solves the patient's problem for them ("You should probably find a new job."); it implies "I know best" and fosters dependency rather than building the patient's own problem-solving skills.

A nontherapeutic communication response in which the nurse endorses a patient's opinion or behavior as objectively "good" or correct; it casts the nurse as the judge of right and wrong and can make it harder for the patient to later change their view without feeling they are disappointing the nurse.
A therapeutic communication technique that lets the patient choose the topic of conversation ("Where would you like to begin?" "What's on your mind today?"); patient-centered and nondirective.

A therapeutic communication technique that shares facts relevant to the patient's care ("Your medication may make your mouth dry; sips of water help."); builds trust and reduces anxiety caused by uncertainty.

A 0–100 clinician rating of a patient's psychological, social, and occupational functioning, with lower scores indicating more severe impairment (≤40 = serious impairment); formerly Axis V of the DSM-IV-TR multiaxial system, removed in DSM-5 for poor reliability but still used in this course's care-plan assignment and replaced in DSM-5 Section III by the WHODAS 2.0. See WHODAS 2.0.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 36, p.1760–1761; Syllabus p.27; Unit 2

terms.html: Exaggerating one's own importance, ranging from unusual self-confidence to a fixed grandiose delusion (believing oneself to be a deity or celebrity); a core symptom of mania.

A legal standard for involuntary commitment meaning a person, because of a mental health disorder (or, under California's SB 43, a severe substance use disorder), is unable to provide for their own basic personal needs such as food, clothing, or shelter. See 5150, LPS conservatorship.
terms.source: general knowledge; Boyd 7e Ch 4, p.121–122; Unit 1

terms.html: The natural, intense physical, emotional, social, and cognitive reaction to the death of a loved one. Contrast: bereavement (the longer coping process) and mourning (the outward, often culturally shaped expression of grief).
Two or more people who develop interactive relationships and share at least one common goal or issue; a group develops its own "personality," patterns of interaction, and behavioral rules.
A member's positive relationship to the group's therapist and other members; one of Yalom's 11 curative factors, distinct from — but related to — the general group concept of cohesion.
The verbal and nonverbal interactions that occur within a group, a concept whose theoretical basis is attributed to Kurt Lewin.
The development and accumulation of session-to-session member interactions that move a group toward its therapeutic goals.
Collective, underlying concerns or feelings expressed repeatedly by group members in different ways across a session.

A group's tendency to avoid conflict and converge on a single, normative pattern of thinking that often mirrors the leader's views; more likely with a respected or persuasive leader, a closed leadership style, external threat, and time pressure. Contrast: cohesion.
The time required for a drug's plasma level to fall by 50%; steady-state blood level is generally reached after 4–5 half-lives of consistent dosing.

A perceptual experience in any sensory modality that occurs without an external stimulus; auditory hallucinations are most common in schizophrenia. Contrast: delusion (a false belief) and illusion (a misperception of a stimulus that really exists).
A class of drugs (LSD, psilocybin, PCP, ketamine) that produce euphoria or dysphoria, altered body image, distorted perception, and impaired judgment.
A 14-item clinician-rated scale for the severity of anxiety symptoms.
A clinician-rated scale for depression severity.

terms.term: HBIPS (Joint Commission inpatient psychiatric core measures)
names: Joint Commission inpatient psychiatric core measures
terms.html: A standardized set of quality measures for inpatient psychiatric units, including admission screening for violence risk, substance use, and trauma history; hours of restraint and seclusion use; and justification for discharge on multiple antipsychotics.
A pragmatic public health and clinical approach that treats any reduction in high-risk substance use or behavior as meaningful progress, rather than requiring total abstinence.
A 27-item screening tool for somatization that assesses dissatisfaction with care, frustration, high health care utilization, health worry, distress, and discordant communication with providers.

A person's ability to use reading, writing, verbal, and numerical skills to obtain, understand, and act on health information; nurses should use "universal precautions," assuming any patient may struggle regardless of education level.

terms.term: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, 1996)
names: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
terms.html: The federal law requiring patient authorization to release health information except for treatment, payment, and health care operations; psychotherapy notes require specific separate patient permission, and any authorization must state exactly what is released, why, to whom, and for how long. See Exceptions to confidentiality.

The body's tendency, described by Walter Cannon, to resist physiologic change and keep internal functions consistent, coordinated, and stable. Contrast: allostasis, the active adaptive process by which the body achieves homeostasis under changing demands.
The belief that bad events will occur and that one's situation will not improve; a strong predictor of suicide risk.
A healthy defense mechanism that emphasizes the amusing side of a stressful situation (joking right after an embarrassing moment).

A subtype of delirium with agitation and heightened psychomotor and autonomic arousal. Contrast: hypoactive delirium (somnolence and psychomotor retardation, the most common subtype and the most often missed) and mixed delirium (alternating between the two).
Inappropriate, socially unacceptable sexual behavior that is uncharacteristic of a person's premorbid behavior; seen in advanced dementia and in mania.
A stress-response system on permanent alert — constantly scanning for danger, startling easily, irritability, and poor sleep; a core cluster of PTSD symptoms.
Screaming, cursing, moaning, groaning, or verbal repetitiveness; a behavioral symptom common in late-stage Alzheimer disease.
An acid-base disturbance caused by losing stomach (hydrochloric) acid through repeated vomiting, as in bulimia nervosa or purging anorexia.
Reduced blood flow and glucose metabolism in the prefrontal cortex; a proposed biologic contributor to the cognitive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia.
A milder form of mania in which judgment remains fundamentally intact and functioning is not severely impaired; the hallmark feature of bipolar II disorder. Contrast: mania.
Illness or injury caused by medical treatment itself; a risk of the repeated procedures, tests, and surgeries that patients with somatic symptom disorder may pursue.

Sigmund Freud's three components of the personality structure — the id (unconscious instinctual drives seeking immediate pleasure), the ego (the rational, reality-testing part of the mind that mediates between the id's demands and reality, and that deploys defense mechanisms), and the superego (the internalized conscience and parental/societal rules). See Freud's structural model of personality.

A defense mechanism in which exaggerated positive qualities are attributed to another person (a new romantic partner "has no faults"); often paired with devaluation in borderline personality disorder.

A defense mechanism in which a person takes on the traits of an admired figure (identification) or internalizes that person's values and standards as their own (introjection) — for example, a teen dresses and talks like a favorite nurse.
Loss of the capacity for self-definition and commitment to stable values, goals, or relationships; seen in borderline personality disorder.

Preoccupation with having or developing a serious illness, with minimal or no actual somatic symptoms, persisting despite medical reassurance; the DSM-5 replacement for the outdated term hypochondriasis.

A misperception or exaggeration of a stimulus that actually exists (mistaking a coat rack for a person, or a husband for his own father); it becomes a delusion only if the mistaken belief hardens and persists despite correction. Contrast: hallucination (no real stimulus at all) and delusion (a fixed false belief).
The key diagnostic feature of delirium — reduced awareness of the environment and an inability to focus, sustain, or shift attention.

Attitudes or stereotypes that affect understanding, actions, and decisions unconsciously; activated involuntarily and without the person's awareness or intentional control. Health care providers have the same level of implicit bias as the general population. Contrast: explicit bias, which is conscious and intentional.
terms.source: Lecture: Implicit Bias and Mental Health Stigma; general knowledge for Joint Commission 2022 definition; Unit 1

terms.html: A behavioral technique in which the therapist presents vivid, highly anxiety-provoking imagery of the feared scene, rather than exposing the patient to the real object.

A category of disorders marked by an inability to resist an impulse or temptation to perform a harmful act, with mounting tension before the act, gratification or relief during it, and often remorse afterward (examples: intermittent explosive disorder, kleptomania, pyromania).
Lashing out in the heat of anger or anxiety, without planning. Contrast: instrumental aggression, which is premeditated and goal-directed.
Emotional expression that is incongruent with the content of one's thoughts or speech, such as laughing while describing a sad event.

The number of new cases of a disorder that occur within a defined time period, usually 1 year. Contrast: prevalence, the number of all existing cases at a given point in time, regardless of when they began.
A group leadership style in which the leader mainly reflects members' own discussion and offers little direction. Contrast: direct leadership.

Group roles adopted to meet a member's own personal needs rather than the group's goals, which detract from group functioning (aggressor, blocker, dominator, recognition seeker). Contrast: task roles and maintenance roles.
Unofficial member positions, each carrying implicit rights and duties, that either help or hinder group process (task roles, maintenance roles, individual roles). Contrast: formal group roles.

The legal and ethical process ensuring a patient understands the diagnosis, the nature and purpose of a proposed treatment, its risks and benefits, alternatives, and the consequences of refusing treatment, and voluntarily agrees to it; requires competence and voluntariness, and a signature alone does not constitute informed consent.
Volatile organic solvents, aerosols, fuel gases, and nitrites that are inhaled to produce rapid CNS depression and euphoria; carry a risk of sudden sniffing death.
A pattern, seen in some personality disorders, of repeated significant trauma and loss combined with an inability to fully experience and resolve the grief.
Awareness of one's own thoughts, feelings, motivations, and illness, and of how one's behavior appears to others; many patients with psychosis lack insight.
The forced long-term confinement of psychiatric patients in large state facilities, roughly 1900–1955, with consistently negative outcomes for patients. Contrast: deinstitutionalization.
Premeditated, goal-directed aggression used deliberately to achieve an end. Contrast: impulsive aggression.

A defense mechanism in which a person uses abstract thinking or technical, clinical-sounding language to avoid directly experiencing or expressing feelings (explaining "relationship dynamics" with no visible emotion right after a breakup).
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 10, p.341; Syllabus p.134; Unit 3, 8

terms.html: Recurrent aggressive outbursts (assault or property destruction) that are grossly out of proportion to the provocation.
A learned association between an internal bodily sensation (dizziness, palpitations) and an impending panic attack, which can trigger panic even without an external trigger.

A therapeutic communication technique that names the underlying feeling behind a patient's words (Patient: "I have nothing to live for." Nurse: "Are you suggesting that life seems without meaning?"); can open a direct suicide assessment.
A reversible, substance-specific syndrome caused by recent use of a substance; for alcohol, measured by blood alcohol level (BAL).

A social or family setting in which a person's emotional responses are habitually dismissed, trivialized, punished, or discredited; a proposed developmental contributor to borderline personality disorder.

Court-ordered psychiatric treatment without the patient's consent; most state statutes require evidence of a mental disorder plus danger to self, danger to others, or grave disability. See 5150, Least restrictive environment. Contrast: voluntary admission.
A defense mechanism in which the facts of a traumatic event are remembered, but the emotions connected to it are separated off (recounting details of an assault calmly, with no apparent feeling).

The MSE component assessing a patient's ability to reach a logical decision and choose an appropriate course of action, often tested with a scenario ("What would you do if you found a bag of money outside a bank?").
The fair distribution of care and resources, including equal access for patients regardless of mental illness, homelessness, or incarceration status.

A theory of bipolar disorder in which repeated subthreshold stressors in a genetically predisposed person produce mood episodes of increasing intensity over time; each episode sensitizes the brain to the next, until episodes eventually occur with little or no outside stressor.
An impulse-control disorder marked by a recurrent, irresistible urge to steal items that are not needed and that the person could otherwise afford.
The chronic phase of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, following untreated Wernicke encephalopathy, marked by an inability to acquire new information, amnesia, and confabulation.
A notable lack of concern or emotional distress about the nature or implications of one's own conversion disorder symptoms, despite seemingly severe disability (such as paralysis).
Avoiding mental health treatment or a diagnosis specifically to escape the stigmatizing label attached to it; one of the three forms of stigma (with public stigma and self-stigma).
Fine, soft, baby-like body hair that grows over the trunk and limbs in starvation, a compensatory response to low body fat and impaired thermoregulation.

The legal right to be treated in the least restrictive setting that is safe and effective — established in Dixon v. Weinberger (1975) and reinforced by Olmstead v. L.C. (1999) — meaning a person cannot be confined to an institution, medicated unnecessarily, or secluded/restrained if a less restrictive option would work. The ladder of restrictiveness runs: verbal de-escalation → PRN oral medication → time-out/quiet room → seclusion → physical restraint (fewest points needed) → chemical restraint.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 4, p.118; Ch 5, p.141; Unit 1, 10

terms.html: The probability that a suicide attempt will actually be completed, based on the seriousness of the person's intent and the likelihood that the chosen method will succeed (a firearm plan is more lethal than superficial cutting).

Peplau's four-level continuum used to guide nursing intervention. Mild anxiety widens perception slightly, keeps the person alert, and allows learning. Moderate anxiety narrows the perceptual field with selective inattention, but the person can still attend if redirected. Severe anxiety greatly reduces the perceptual field, blocks learning and problem-solving, and produces marked relief behaviors. Panic reduces perception to one blown-up detail, causes dissociation and loss of logical function, and can precede a psychotic break; safety is the priority intervention.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 27, p.1136; Ch 7, p.223; Unit 8

terms.html: A four-stage progression of auditory hallucination severity, paralleling the levels of anxiety: Stage I "comforting" (moderate anxiety, nonpsychotic), Stage II "condemning" (severe anxiety), Stage III "controlling" (severe anxiety, psychotic; the person obeys the voices), Stage IV "conquering" (panic level; high risk for suicide or homicide). Anxiety reduction is the key intervention for interrupting hallucinations at any stage.

Legal responsibility for harm caused by negligence or malpractice — for example, failing to protect a suicidal patient, failing to warn an identifiable victim, improper use of restraint, giving medication without legal authority, breaching confidentiality, or abandonment.
Scheduled exposure to bright artificial light, an evidence-based treatment for mild-to-moderate seasonal, nonpsychotic winter depression that can be as effective as antidepressant medication.

A nontherapeutic communication response that takes a patient's figurative or symbolic statement at face value, missing the feeling it conveys (Patient: "My insides are rotting." Nurse: "Then you need to see a GI doctor.").
Sudden shifts in topic with no apparent logical link to what came before; a thought-process disorder seen in schizophrenia.

A California court-ordered Lanterman-Petris-Short Act conservatorship appointing a conservator for a person who remains gravely disabled by mental illness, authorizing the conservator to consent to psychiatric treatment and placement on the person's behalf; lasts up to 1 year and is renewable; a temporary LPS conservatorship can last up to 30 days pending the formal hearing.
Group roles that keep the group together and maintain cohesion — harmonizer, compromiser, standard setter. Contrast: task roles and individual roles.
A therapeutic communication technique that draws attention to behavior the patient may not have noticed ("You appear tense." "You are trembling and perspiring. When did this start?").
A nontherapeutic communication response using an empty, automatic phrase ("Keep your chin up." "It's for your own good.") that shows the nurse isn't really listening.

The intentional production or exaggeration of symptoms motivated by a specific, external, self-serving goal (obtaining disability payments, avoiding work or legal consequences). Contrast: factitious disorder, which has no external goal — only the internal desire to occupy the sick role.
Professional negligence — a health care provider's failure to meet the accepted standard of care, resulting in patient harm. See Negligence.

A professional (including every nurse) who is legally required to report suspected child abuse, elder abuse, or dependent-adult abuse to the appropriate authorities; this duty overrides ordinary confidentiality.

The set of legal exceptions requiring a clinician to break confidentiality — threats of harm to an identifiable person (duty to warn/protect), suicide risk, child/elder/dependent-adult abuse, certain court orders, specific communicable diseases, and medical emergencies. See Duty to warn, Mandated reporter.

A primary symptom of bipolar disorders — an abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy, lasting at least 1 week (or any duration if hospitalization is required), that causes marked impairment in functioning. Contrast: hypomania.

Abraham Maslow's humanistic model ranking human needs from most to least basic — physiologic needs (food, water, sleep, elimination) → safety and security → love and belonging → esteem → self-actualization — with lower needs generally requiring satisfaction before higher ones can be addressed. Nursing application: feed, hydrate, and ensure the safety of a manic or psychotic patient before attempting insight-oriented work.

The facet of cognition concerned with retaining and recalling past experiences; the hippocampus is key to transferring information from short-term to long-term storage. Memory spheres tested on the MSE are immediate/recall, short-term (3 words recalled at 5 and 15 minutes), recent (events within recent months), and remote (events from years ago, verified with family).
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 39, p.1875; Ch 11, p.389; Unit 2, 11

terms.html: A clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion regulation, or behavior that reflects dysfunction in underlying psychological, biologic, or developmental processes, usually accompanied by distress or impaired functioning; defined by clusters of symptoms, not a specific laboratory test.
Emotional and psychological well-being that allows a person to interact effectively with others, manage ordinary life stress, and perceive their surroundings realistically. Contrast: mental disorder.

An organized, systematic snapshot of a patient's current psychiatric condition — general observations, orientation, mood, affect, speech, thought process, thought content, perception, cognition, insight, and judgment — that establishes a baseline and a written record for later comparison.

The capacity to understand the mental states — thoughts, feelings, intentions — of oneself and others. Mentalization-based therapy (MBT) is a psychodynamic treatment, often used for borderline personality disorder, that strengthens this capacity.

A harm-reduction treatment for opioid use disorder using a daily stabilized dose of methadone, a long-acting opioid agonist, to satisfy craving and prevent withdrawal without producing heroin's intense high.

A modest decline in one or more cognitive domains that does not interfere with the person's independence in daily activities, in contrast to major neurocognitive disorder (dementia), which does; subtypes are amnestic (memory-predominant) and nonamnestic.

The deliberate use of a stable, coherent social and physical environment — through containment, validation, structured interaction, and open communication — as a therapeutic tool on an inpatient unit.
A brief dementia screening tool combining 3-word recall with a clock-drawing task; scored 0–5, with a score below 3 (some protocols use below 4) considered a positive screen requiring further workup.
A solution-focused brief therapy technique in which the patient imagines that the problem disappeared overnight and describes, in concrete detail, what would be different the next morning.
Mania and depression occurring at the same time, producing extreme anxiety, agitation, irritability, and a particularly high suicide risk.

A 30-point cognitive screening tool assessing orientation, registration, attention/calculation, recall, language, and copying; scores of 24–30 are usually normal, 18–23 indicate mild impairment, and 0–17 indicate severe impairment (interpretation should be adjusted for the patient's education level).

An anxiety level in which the perceptual field narrows and the person shows selective inattention, but can still attend to the environment if directed; the person can usually say "I am anxious." See Levels of anxiety.
A pervasive, sustained emotional state the patient reports and that colors perception of the world; described as euthymic, euphoric, dysphoric, or labile. Contrast: affect.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 11, p.387; Ch 25, p.1009; Unit 2, 7

terms.html: Rapid shifts in mood with little or no change in the external triggering events; an extreme form is rapid cycling.
The 1790–1900 asylum reform movement (led by Pinel, Tuke, and the Quakers) that treated patients with kindness, compassion, and pleasant surroundings instead of chains and punishment.
A goal-oriented attitude that propels and sustains behavior change, which is more likely to succeed when appropriate support and treatment are available.
A collaborative, patient-centered counseling method that elicits and strengthens a patient's own reasons for change ("change talk") while rolling with — rather than confronting — resistance.
A lessening or loss of normal function seen in schizophrenia — diminished emotional expression (flat/blunted affect), alogia, avolition, anhedonia, and asociality. Contrast: positive symptoms.
A breach of a professional's duty of reasonable care that causes injury; the five elements are duty, breach, cause in fact, proximate cause, and damages. See Malpractice.
A made-up word that has no conventional or shared meaning; a thought-process disorder seen in schizophrenia.

A culturally sanctioned Chinese idiom of distress expressed as headaches, insomnia, dizziness, body aches, poor memory, weakness, and low energy, rather than through the Western vocabulary of depression.

An acquired decline from a person's previous level of cognitive function across one or more domains — attention, executive function, learning/memory, language, perceptual-motor, and social cognition — that includes delirium, mild neurocognitive impairment, and major neurocognitive disorder (dementia).

A dementia with cognitive decline accompanied by visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, parkinsonian motor features, and fluctuating cognition; patients are extremely sensitive to the side effects of antipsychotics, which should be used with great caution.

Twisted threads of abnormal tau protein that accumulate inside neurons, collapsing the cell's internal transport system (microtubules) and leading to cell death; a hallmark pathology of Alzheimer disease along with beta-amyloid plaques.

A life-threatening, idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotic medication marked by severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia (often 101–103°F, sometimes higher), autonomic instability, and altered mental status; a medical emergency requiring immediate discontinuation of the antipsychotic and supportive care.
The brain's continuous modulation of neuronal structure and function in response to experience and the environment.
A small signaling molecule, released from a presynaptic neuron, that directly or indirectly controls the opening or closing of ion channels on a receiving cell, allowing nerve cells to communicate.

terms.term: NGRI (not guilty by reason of insanity)
names: not guilty by reason of insanity
terms.html: A legal verdict stating the defendant was not criminally responsible for an act because a mental disorder left them unable to tell right from wrong or to control their actions at the time; the person is committed to a secure psychiatric hospital rather than prison. Contrast: GBMI.
A legal verdict in which the defendant is convicted and sent to the correctional system but also receives psychiatric treatment while incarcerated. Contrast: NGRI.
Recurrent episodes of eating after waking from sleep, or excessive eating after the evening meal, with awareness and recall of the eating, accompanied by distress, poor sleep, and morning anorexia.
