A delusion with a plausible theme, such as jealousy or persecution, that could theoretically happen even though it isn't true for this person. Contrast: bizarre delusion.
The ethical duty to never intentionally cause harm — for example, avoiding unnecessary restraint and monitoring for medication side effects. Contrast: beneficence.
A nurse-patient relationship pattern in which both parties keep changing their approach without finding common ground, and the relationship ends in mutual withdrawal rather than resolution.
Gestures, facial expression, posture, eye contact, and body movement, which often communicate more than the spoken word; when verbal and nonverbal messages conflict, believe the nonverbal message.
Anxiety of a realistic intensity and duration for the actual situation, followed by typical relief behaviors; Peplau's baseline against which pathological anxiety is measured.
Excessive, unwanted, intrusive, and persistent thoughts, impulses, or images that cause marked anxiety and are not under the person's voluntary control. Contrast: compulsions.
A dystonic reaction in which the eyes are involuntarily pulled upward. Related: torticollis (head pulled to the side) and retrocollis (head pulled back); all are forms of acute dystonia.
A therapeutic communication technique that encourages the patient to keep talking without directing the content ("Tell me more about that." "Go on.").
A therapeutic communication technique in which the nurse offers their presence without conditions ("I'll sit with you for a while.").
A therapy group in which new members may join and existing members may leave at different sessions over time; typical of inpatient units. Contrast: closed group.

An interview question that invites the patient to elaborate and reveals how the patient thinks and responds; typically used to start an interview. Contrast: closed-ended question, used to obtain specific facts and clarify details.

A therapeutic communication technique that invites the patient to complete a thought in their own words ("Trust means…"), encouraging exploration. Contrast: open-ended question, used to start an interview more broadly.

B. F. Skinner's model of learning in which a behavior that is followed by reinforcement (reward) tends to be repeated, while a behavior that is ignored or punished tends to fade (extinction); the basis for token economies, behavior modification programs, and extinguishing attention-seeking behavior on an inpatient unit.

Any substance that binds opioid receptors with agonist action, including natural opiates (morphine, codeine), semisynthetic agents (oxycodone, hydrocodone), and synthetic agents (fentanyl, methadone).
Awareness of person, place, and time (including date and, if the exact date is unknown, the correct season); not knowing the year or one's location indicates considerable confusion.

The first phase of the nurse-patient relationship, in which the nurse introduces themselves, explains the purpose and boundaries of the relationship (confidentiality limits, time, frequency, planned length), gathers data, and builds trust; termination is discussed starting on day one. An early "honeymoon" period is often followed by testing behaviors (lateness, missed sessions, anger). See Peplau's phases.
Health experiences reported by the patient or observed by the nurse that can be attributed to nursing care; written to be concise, neutral, and mutually developed with the patient.
Cellular damage from reactive free radicals affecting proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids; one hypothesized mechanism of neuronal injury in Alzheimer disease.

An extremely overwhelming, intense form of anxiety occurring in response to a real or perceived life-threatening situation; the most severe level on the anxiety continuum. See Levels of anxiety, Panic attack.

An abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes (usually about 10, up to 30), accompanied by at least 4 of 13 characteristic physical or cognitive symptoms (palpitations, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, chills/hot flashes, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control or dying).

A behavioral treatment in which the patient is intentionally exposed to panic-like physical sensations (through exercise, such as spinning or hyperventilating), combined with breathing retraining and cognitive restructuring, to break the fear of the sensations themselves.
A diagnosis defined by recurrent, unexpected panic attacks, followed by at least 1 month of persistent worry about having more attacks or of maladaptive behavior change meant to avoid them.
Unrealistic suspiciousness and guardedness toward others, often accompanied by grandiosity.
Deliberate self-injury performed with the intent to harm — but not necessarily kill — oneself; common in borderline personality disorder.
A suicidal gesture — an apparent suicide attempt in which death is not the actual aim; always taken seriously because intent can be misjudged and the act can still be lethal.
A drug that binds a receptor but produces only a weak intrinsic activity/response compared with a full agonist, such as the aripiprazole class of antipsychotics (dopamine partial agonists).
A defense mechanism expressing indirect hostility behind a front of outward compliance, such as secretly sabotaging a coworker rather than confronting them directly.
An ANA-endorsed (1982) confidential program offering consultation, referral, and monitoring for nurses impaired by a substance use disorder, as an alternative to disciplinary board action.
Hildegard Peplau's six roles a psychiatric nurse moves through within the therapeutic relationship — stranger, resource person, teacher, counselor, surrogate, and leader.

terms.term: Peplau's phases of the nurse-patient relationship
names: Peplau's phases of the nurse-patient relationship
terms.html: Four sequential phases — Orientation (building trust, setting boundaries), Identification (patient explores feelings and identifies with the nurse), Exploitation (patient fully uses the relationship to work on problems; transference/countertransference are most active here), Resolution (termination; patient gives up old behaviors, nurse promotes self-care and independence). Boyd 7e condenses these into three phases — Orientation, Working (combining Identification and Exploitation), and Resolution. See Orientation phase, Working phase, Resolution phase.
terms.source: Syllabus p.127; Boyd 7e Ch 10, p.350–355; Unit 3

terms.html: Holding excessively high personal standards combined with intense concern over mistakes and their effect on self-worth; typically predates and predisposes to eating disorders.
Erosion of tooth enamel, especially on the front teeth, caused by repeated exposure to stomach acid during self-induced vomiting.

Involuntary, pathological repetition of a particular response (word, phrase, or action) despite the absence or cessation of the stimulus that originally prompted it; seen in schizophrenia and some neurocognitive disorders.
Chronic, low-grade depressive symptoms present most of the day for at least 2 years in adults (1 year in children and adolescents).
A complex, largely unconscious pattern of characteristics that forms a person's distinctive way of perceiving, feeling, thinking, coping, and behaving.

An enduring pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates markedly from cultural expectations, is pervasive and inflexible across situations, begins by adolescence or early adulthood, remains stable over time, and causes significant distress or functional impairment.
Prominent, consistent aspects of personality displayed across a wide range of social and personal situations; shaped by biology, psychological experience, and environment.
The study of the action or effect of a drug on the living organism — what the drug does to the body. Contrast: pharmacokinetics.
The study of how an individual's genetic makeup affects their response to medications, including identifying poor versus rapid (ultra-rapid) drug metabolizers.
The processes by which a drug is absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and eliminated by the body — what the body does to the drug. Contrast: pharmacodynamics.

A 9-item self-report screening tool for depression severity, scored 0–3 per item for a total of 0–27: 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe, 20–27 severe; any positive answer on item 9 (thoughts of death or self-harm) requires an immediate suicide risk assessment regardless of the total score.

An expected, often inevitable physiologic adaptation to certain medications taken as prescribed (opioids, beta-blockers, antidepressants, benzodiazepines), requiring a gradual taper rather than abrupt discontinuation; not the same as addiction.

terms.term: Placing the event in time or sequence
names: Placing the event in time or sequence
terms.html: A therapeutic communication technique that clarifies cause-and-effect and identifies triggers ("What happened just before you felt that way?").

Compulsive, excessive fluid drinking, which in chronic psychosis can cause life-threatening dilutional hyponatremia (water intoxication); a psychiatric emergency requiring fluid restriction and close monitoring.
The use of five or more medications, or of duplicate or interacting drugs, or drugs prescribed to treat the adverse effects of other drugs; highly prevalent, and particularly risky, in older adults.
Rehearsed, realistic coping statements used to manage anxiety ("This is only anxiety, and it will pass").
An excess or distortion of normal function seen in psychosis — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior. Contrast: negative symptoms.

The dose of a drug required to produce a given effect; a highly potent drug produces its effect at a low dose. Contrast: efficacy, the drug's actual ability to produce the intended therapeutic response regardless of dose.
Grief experienced before an expected death occurs, such as in caregivers of a person with advanced dementia or terminal illness.
Recurring mood swings, sadness, irritability, or rejection sensitivity concentrated in the final week before menses, improving within a few days after menses begins.
Age-related hearing loss, especially for high-pitched sounds; can be mistaken for cognitive impairment in older adults. Nursing tip: lower your voice pitch rather than shouting.
A therapeutic communication technique that gently and simply states what is actually true ("I see no one else in the room.") without arguing with the patient's hallucination or delusion.
Speech that is more rapid and talkative than usual and is often difficult to interrupt; a classic sign of mania.
See Incidence (contrast pair).

In the transactional stress model, the first step of judging whether an event is a threat, a harm, or a challenge, and whether it is relevant to one's values and commitments. Contrast: secondary appraisal.

In somatic symptom and conversion disorders, the relief of anxiety obtained by keeping an internal psychological conflict out of conscious awareness by converting it into a physical symptom. Contrast: secondary gain.
The part of a person's life not governed by society or government intrusion. Contrast: confidentiality, the professional's ethical duty not to disclose information once it has been shared.
A unit-based behavioral system in which patients earn freedoms (passes, phone use, outdoor time) through appropriate, safe behavior, reinforcing unit rules within milieu therapy.
A nontherapeutic communication response involving persistent questioning about details a patient is not ready to share; it feels invasive and makes the patient defensive.
A coping strategy that directly addresses the source of stress in an effort to solve the problem itself. Contrast: emotion-focused coping.

A verbatim written record of a nurse-patient interaction, reconstructed from memory immediately afterward, including both parties' verbal and nonverbal behavior, followed by the nurse's analysis of the techniques used.
The early stage of subtle changes and symptoms that come before the full onset of a disorder, such as schizophrenia.

The limits that keep a therapeutic relationship focused on the patient's needs and prevent exploitation of the patient; warning signs of a boundary problem include accepting gifts, keeping secrets from the team, spending extra unscheduled time with one patient, or feeling you alone understand the patient. See Boundaries.
A defense mechanism in which a person attributes their own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone else (a patient who secretly wants to hit others instead insists that staff want to hurt him).

A defense mechanism, prominent in borderline personality disorder, in which overwhelming feelings are unconsciously projected onto a significant other, with the unconscious hope that the other person will manage them — a process that typically leads to more rejection rather than relief.

A nontherapeutic communication response ("I won't tell anyone.") that can never actually be honored when safety is involved — suicide risk, violence toward others, or abuse — and should never be offered to a patient.
The attachment of a drug to plasma proteins; only the unbound, "free" fraction of a drug is pharmacologically active, and protein binding prolongs a drug's duration of action.
Moving repeatedly from one health care provider to another seeking new medications, hospitalizations, or surgeries; a pattern seen in somatic symptom disorder.
Telling fascinating, partly true and partly false stories of personal triumph or dramatic events; a core feature of factitious disorder.

A drug-induced extrapyramidal syndrome mimicking Parkinson disease — rigidity, akinesia (slowed movement), tremor, and mask-like facial expression — caused by antipsychotic dopamine blockade; the risk is greatest in older adults.

A document made while a person is competent, signed by the patient and two witnesses, stating preferences for future psychiatric crisis care (preferred medications, hospitals, treatments); a physician can override a PAD only when a court orders it and the patient's decision-making is clearly distorted by their mental illness, and the patient may revoke it while competent.

The nursing specialty that promotes mental health by assessing, diagnosing, and treating behavioral problems, mental disorders, and comorbid conditions across the lifespan, through the purposeful use of self combined with nursing, psychosocial, and neurobiological evidence.
Emotional injury resulting from an overwhelmingly stressful event that threatens a person's survival or sense of safety.
An observable increase (agitation) or decrease (retardation) in motor activity accompanying a mood episode — a measurable sign, not merely a subjective feeling.
The study of cytokines as chemical messengers linking the immune system and the nervous system; elevated cytokines are associated with depression and cognitive impairment.
A state in which a person experiences hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized thoughts, speech, or behavior; the key diagnostic feature of schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
An older, now-discouraged term implying a purely psychological origin for a physical illness; it perpetuates the stigma that such symptoms are "not real."

A psychiatric disorder following exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, with symptoms across four clusters — intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in mood and cognition, and marked changes in arousal/reactivity — lasting more than 1 month. Contrast: acute stress disorder (same symptom profile but resolving within 1 month).
Deliberately emptying the stomach or bowel — through self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse, diuretic misuse, or enemas — to compensate for eating.
Recurrent purging at least weekly after eating normal (not binge-sized) amounts of food, accompanied by intense fear of weight gain, without the binge eating seen in bulimia nervosa.

An impulse-control disorder marked by repeated, deliberate fire setting, with tension or arousal beforehand and gratification or relief from watching the fire; not motivated by anger, financial gain, or ideology.

An extreme form of mood lability in bipolar disorder — continuous cycling between subthreshold mania and depression, or between hypomania and depression, typically defined as 4 or more mood episodes within a year.
Interpersonal harmony marked by mutual understanding and respect, built through warmth, a nonjudgmental attitude, and genuine understanding of the patient.

Albert Ellis's form of cognitive behavioral therapy that identifies and disputes irrational, absolute beliefs ("musts" and "shoulds") that generate emotional distress, replacing them with more reasonable, rational thoughts. See ABCDE.
A defense mechanism offering a socially acceptable but false explanation for one's own behavior ("She left because she was beneath me socially").
A defense mechanism in which a person acts in a way that is the direct opposite of what they actually feel (a person who dislikes a coworker is overly sweet to her).
Repeating a stress appraisal after a coping strategy has been tried, giving feedback that allows the person to adjust their approach.
A sharp increase in anxiety that occurs after the peak effect of a short-acting benzodiazepine wears off, often worse than the original anxiety; a reason to taper benzodiazepines slowly.

A process of change through which a person improves their health and wellness, lives a self-directed life, and strives toward their full potential; nonlinear, and described as something that "emerges from hope."
A psychiatric assessment conducted collaboratively with the patient that explicitly includes the patient's strengths and sources of wellness, not only problems and deficits.
The belief that neutral external stimuli — a television commentator, a stranger's glance — carry a special, personal meaning directed at oneself.
Nutritional rehabilitation of a malnourished patient, typically the most important and most medically difficult early intervention for anorexia nervosa.

A severe electrolyte disturbance (hypophosphatemia occurs first, with hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia) during the refeeding of a malnourished patient, which can lead to fluid overload and respiratory or cardiac failure if refeeding proceeds too quickly.

A therapeutic communication technique that returns the patient's own question or feeling back to them rather than giving an opinion (Patient: "Should I go home for the weekend?" Nurse: "Do you think you should?"); avoids the nurse giving approval or judgment.
A cognitive technique that changes the way a situation or a person is viewed, such as by replacing rigid "should" statements with more flexible language.

A defense mechanism in which a person returns to an earlier, more immature developmental level under stress (a hospitalized adult curls up and sucks their thumb; a toilet-trained 4-year-old wets the bed after a sibling is born).
A nontherapeutic communication response that closes off a topic ("Let's not talk about that."); the patient is left feeling dismissed.

The recurrence of substance use after a significant period of abstinence beyond the initial detoxification period; an expected, common event in the course of a chronic substance use disorder, not a moral failure.
Behaviors, often used automatically and outside conscious awareness, that reduce anxiety (pacing, repetitive hand movements); especially prominent at severe and panic levels of anxiety.

A defense mechanism involving the unconscious blocking of painful thoughts or memories from awareness (no conscious memory of a traumatic event, but anxiety when near the place it occurred). Contrast: suppression, which is a conscious, deliberate decision to set a problem aside.
The capacity to withstand stress and catastrophe without lasting psychological damage; it develops over time from a combination of internal traits and external supports, and can be strengthened.

The final, termination phase of the nurse-patient relationship, in which the patient gives up old maladaptive behaviors and uses new skills, the nurse promotes self-care and makes referrals, and feelings about ending the relationship (sadness, anger, attempts to prolong contact) are acknowledged without being reopened. See Peplau's phases.

A therapeutic communication technique that repeats back the main idea of what the patient said in different words (Patient: "I hate this place. I don't belong here." Nurse: "You don't want to be here."); shows what was heard and invites clarification.

Any manual, physical, or mechanical method, device, or material that immobilizes or reduces a patient's ability to move freely; used only as a last resort for imminent danger to self or others, for the shortest possible time, after less restrictive measures have failed. See Chemical restraint, Seclusion, Least restrictive environment.
An anorexia nervosa subtype marked by weight loss through dieting, fasting, or excessive exercise, with no recurrent binge eating or purging in the last 3 months. Contrast: binge-eating/purging type.

A California legal procedure (from Riese v. St. Mary's Hospital, 1987) under which an involuntarily held patient who refuses antipsychotic medication, outside an emergency, gets a hearing before a hearing officer or judge to determine whether the patient lacks the capacity to consent to or refuse that medication; if capacity is lacking, medication may be given over the patient's objection for the duration of the current hold.
A patient's legal right to decline treatment, including medication, except in a true emergency or as otherwise permitted by law (such as a Riese order).

A systematic evaluation of a patient's risk to safety (suicide, violence toward others, falls, seizures, elopement), risk of developing a disorder, and risk of worsening symptoms; threats of suicide or violence always take priority over other assessment findings.
Compulsions in which objects must be arranged in a certain order, or acts must be performed in a fixed, rigid sequence.
Carl Rogers's humanistic approach built on empathy, genuineness, and unconditional positive regard for the client, providing a nonjudgmental foundation for the therapeutic relationship.
Calluses or scars on the knuckles or back of the hand caused by repeated contact with the teeth during self-induced vomiting; a physical exam clue for bulimia nervosa.

A suicide risk mnemonic — Sex (male), Age (older, especially older white males), Depression, Previous attempts, Ethanol/substance use, Rational thinking loss, Social support lacking, Organized plan, No spouse, Sickness (chronic/debilitating medical illness) — used to flag risk factors for completed suicide.
A solution-focused brief therapy technique in which the patient rates a problem on a scale from 1 (worst) to 10 (problem absent), used to quantify severity and track change over time.

An enduring "life rule" that acts like a filter, allowing only information compatible with one's existing picture of self and world into conscious awareness; schemata develop in early childhood and become relatively fixed by middle childhood.
Personality traits that resemble schizophrenia symptoms but in a milder, subclinical form — magical thinking, perceptual aberrations, odd beliefs — seen in schizotypal personality disorder.
An OCD symptom dimension involving religious or moral intrusive thoughts paired with repetitive compensatory acts, such as repeated confession or prayer rituals.
See Brief intervention / SBIRT.

The involuntary confinement of a patient alone in a room or area from which they are physically prevented from leaving; like restraint, used only as a last resort for imminent danger, for the shortest time necessary. See Least restrictive environment.
Traumatic stress symptoms that develop in a caregiver who is repeatedly exposed to other people's trauma — for example, in nurses who regularly care for suicidal or traumatized patients.
In the transactional stress model, the step of judging whether one has the personal and social resources needed to cope with a perceived threat. Contrast: primary appraisal.
External benefits a person receives from occupying the "sick role" — attention, excusal from responsibilities, or support that might not otherwise be offered. Contrast: primary gain.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 33, p.1563; Syllabus p.149; Unit 12

terms.html: A therapeutic communication technique that checks the nurse's understanding against what the patient actually meant ("I'm not sure I follow." "Let me see if I understand."); prevents misunderstanding. See Validation.
A feature of moderate anxiety — not noticing stimuli outside one's immediate focus of attention, though the person can still attend to them if specifically directed. See Levels of anxiety.

Understanding one's own beliefs, thoughts, motivations, biases, and limits, and how these affect one's interactions with others; requires ongoing introspection and feedback from a trusted colleague or supervisor.
A person's total set of beliefs about themselves, including body image, self-esteem, and personal identity.
The fundamental patient right to autonomy — to accept, refuse, or terminate treatment without coercion, and the right to seek a second opinion or an alternative treatment.

A nurse's deliberate sharing of personal information with a patient; generally avoided in therapeutic relationships, and used only in specific situations with a clear therapeutic purpose. Overuse (excessive self-disclosure) shifts the focus to the nurse and blurs professional boundaries.
Deliberate, direct injury to one's own body, whether or not death is intended; seen across several disorders, including borderline personality disorder. See Parasuicidal behavior.
Keeping a diary of food intake, binge and purge episodes, and the emotional and environmental cues around them; a foundational self-assessment tool for CBT in eating disorders.
The internalization of society's negative stereotypes about one's own mental illness or identity; contributes, along with public stigma, to label avoidance and treatment delay. See Stigma.
terms.source: Lecture: Implicit Bias and Mental Health Stigma; Boyd 7e Ch 2, p.77–79; Unit 1

terms.html: The developmental stage, described in object relations theory, in which a young child develops a stable sense of self, object constancy (the ability to hold onto a positive internal image of a caregiver when they are absent), and the capacity to see both good and bad qualities in the same person; disruption of this stage is linked to borderline personality disorder.

A potentially life-threatening state of serotonin overactivity — mental status change, autonomic instability, neuromuscular hyperactivity (hyperreflexia, clonus), and GI symptoms — most often from combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans).
A learned pattern of illness behavior (reporting symptoms, seeking care, limiting activity) that predictably provokes supportive responses from others.
A deliberate pause in conversation that gives the patient time to organize and express their own thoughts and communicates acceptance; the nurse should not fill silence out of their own anxiety.

A crisis triggered by a specific, identifiable stressful event (illness, job loss, relocation, graduation) that threatens physical or psychosocial integrity. Contrast: developmental crisis and traumatic crisis.
The Saint Louis University Mental Status Examination, an easy-to-administer cognitive screening tool used as an alternative to the MMSE.
A persistent, marked fear of social or performance situations in which the person believes they may be embarrassed, judged negatively, or scrutinized by others.
A person's performance of daily activities within interpersonal, family, and community roles.
The actual set of people with whom a person has personal contact, organized into levels based on closeness (Levels I–III). Contrast: social support, the help that network actually provides.

A theory of bipolar disorder in which disruption of patterned daily social cues (wake time, meal times, first social contact) — cues that normally set the body's circadian clock — increases the likelihood of a mood episode.
The emotional, tangible (practical help), and informational assistance a person receives from their social network. Contrast: social network.

A time-limited therapy approach that focuses on solutions rather than problems, helping the patient envision and build a life without the problem rather than analyzing the problem's origin. See Miracle questions, Exception questions, Scaling questions, Relationship questions, Compliments.

One or more physical symptoms causing persistent distress or significant disruption to daily life for at least 6 months, accompanied by excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to the symptoms; the symptoms may or may not be medically explained. Formerly called hypochondriasis or somatization disorder.
The manifestation of underlying psychological distress as physical symptoms, which may involve actual functional changes in the body, purely somatic descriptions of distress, or both.

A persistent, excessive fear of a specific, circumscribed object or situation (animal, natural environment such as heights or storms, blood-injection-injury, or a specific situation such as flying), out of proportion to any actual danger.

A defense mechanism — and a diagnostic feature of borderline personality disorder — in which a person sees self and others as entirely good or entirely bad, with no ability to integrate both qualities in the same person; clinically, staff members on a unit may be alternately idealized and devalued by the same patient.

A 10-question cognitive screen: 0–2 errors is normal, 3–4 mild impairment, 5–7 moderate impairment, 8 or more severe impairment; allow one additional error for a grade-school education or less, and one fewer error for education beyond high school.

The ANA/APNA/ISPN six standards organizing psychiatric-mental health nursing practice around the nursing process — assessment, diagnosis, outcomes identification, planning, implementation, and evaluation.
Repetitive, purposeless, idiosyncratic movements performed over and over; a catatonic symptom.

Labeling a person as different and linking that label to negative stereotypes, leading to prejudice and discrimination. Public stigma is society's negative attitude toward people with mental illness; self-stigma is the internalization of those attitudes by the affected person; label avoidance is avoiding treatment altogether to escape being labeled.
terms.source: Boyd 7e Ch 2, p.77–79; Lecture: Implicit Bias and Mental Health Stigma; Unit 1

terms.html: Deliberately using language that emphasizes a patient's strengths and resourcefulness ("resourceful; trying to get help") rather than pathologizing, judgmental labels ("manipulative").
A process arising from real or perceived internal or external demands that are appraised as either threatening or benign; the appraisal, not just the event itself, determines the stress response.
A purposeful interaction, or a deliberately consistent staff attitude (such as a matter-of-fact tone), assigned to a patient as part of the therapeutic milieu.

Dementia caused by dysfunction of deep gray and white matter brain structures rather than the cortex itself; tends to disrupt arousal, attention, and motivation more than memory or language. Contrast: cortical dementia.
A mature defense mechanism in which an unacceptable impulse is channeled into a socially acceptable, often productive activity (an angry teen tackles hard on the football field).
Intoxication, withdrawal, or another psychiatric syndrome caused directly by a medication or substance. Contrast: substance use disorder.
Continued substance use despite significant cognitive, behavioral, and physiologic symptoms, reflecting persistent changes in brain circuitry rather than simple willpower failure.

A defense mechanism in which an unattainable goal is replaced with a more attainable (the syllabus specifies "less acceptable") one (a student who can't get into medical school becomes a pharmacist instead).
Death from inhalant abuse that occurs when inhaled fumes displace oxygen in the lungs or trigger a fatal cardiac arrhythmia, even on a first use.
A therapeutic communication technique that proposes a partnership while keeping responsibility with the patient ("Perhaps you and I can discuss it and discover what produces your anxiety.").
Thinking about, planning, or considering one's own death; the mildest point on the suicide risk continuum, but it always requires assessment.
The voluntary act of killing oneself, with either explicit or inferred intent to die.
A nonfatal, self-inflicted destructive act carried out with the intent to die. Contrast: parasuicide, in which death is not actually the goal.

An increase in suicidal behavior following exposure to the suicide of a known person or a publicized celebrity suicide, driven by modeling and media coverage; a reason clinicians counsel careful, nonsensationalized media reporting.

Harry Stack Sullivan's theory that personality is shaped by interpersonal relationships, that psychological health depends on one's patterns of relating to others, that anxiety arises specifically within relationships, and that the self-system functions as an anti-anxiety system; the theoretical foundation for the nurse-patient therapeutic relationship and for milieu therapy.
A therapeutic communication technique that organizes the key points of a session ("Today we talked about your sleep and what makes your voices worse."); often used near the end of an interaction.

Worsening confusion, agitation, and behavioral symptoms in the late afternoon and evening in patients with dementia, related to fatigue and reduced tolerance for environmental stimulation as the day progresses. The term itself is general knowledge; Boyd describes the underlying fatigue-related phenomenon without using this label.
terms.source: general knowledge; Boyd 7e Ch 39, p.1930; Unit 11

terms.html: Compression of the duodenum between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery after loss of the protective fat pad in severe malnutrition, causing epigastric pain, nausea, and intestinal obstruction.
Guilt experienced by a person who survived a traumatic event (disaster, combat, accident) when others did not.

A defense mechanism in which a person makes a conscious, deliberate decision to put a problem aside for later (going to a movie to stop thinking about pending test results). Contrast: repression, which is unconscious. Memory hook: suppression is conscious; repression is unconscious.

Using a word or image to represent a feeling or an event ("bombs and guns" standing in for fear); often highly idiosyncratic and personal in severe mental illness, requiring the nurse to explore the patient's own meaning rather than assume a standard interpretation.
See Empathy (contrast pair).

Real-time, live interaction between patient and provider (video or phone visit). Contrast: asynchronous telehealth ("store-and-forward"), such as email, text messaging, or recorded data sent for later review.
A behavioral technique in which a patient is gradually exposed to feared situations along a patient-rated hierarchy, from least to most feared, combined with relaxation training.
A logical-seeming change of topic that permanently detours away from the original point and never returns to it. Contrast: circumstantiality, which eventually returns to the point.

terms.term: Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California (1974/1976)
names: Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California
terms.html: The landmark California Supreme Court case establishing that a therapist who learns a patient intends to harm an identifiable victim has a duty to warn that victim, broadened on rehearing to a duty to use reasonable care to protect them (which can include warning the victim, notifying police, or hospitalizing the patient); established the modern duty to warn/protect.

A late-appearing, often irreversible movement disorder caused by long-term antipsychotic use, with involuntary, repetitive movements of the mouth, tongue, face, trunk, and limbs (lip smacking, tongue protrusion); monitored with the AIMS scale every 3–6 months; prevalence is 15%–20% overall and 50%–70% in older adults on long-term antipsychotics.
The specific, measurable symptoms a medication is expected to improve; used to judge whether a drug trial is actually working.
Group member roles focused on the group's purpose, which "keep things on task" — information seeker, coordinator, recorder. Contrast: maintenance roles and individual roles.

A natural, neurobiologically based predisposition to express certain feelings and actions; visible in infancy and relatively stable across the lifespan. Contrast: personality, which also incorporates experience and environment.
A stress-response pattern, more common in females, of responding to a stressor with affiliation and caregiving behavior rather than the classic fight-or-flight response.
An ongoing, purposeful process of interaction through which shared meaning emerges between nurse and patient; always patient-focused.

The ratio between a drug's maximum nontoxic dose and its minimum effective dose; a low (narrow) therapeutic index, as with lithium, means the margin between an effective dose and a toxic one is small, requiring close blood-level monitoring.
A sudden, involuntary interruption in the flow of speech or thought before an idea is completed, with no explanation from the patient for the gap; a symptom associated with schizophrenia.
What a patient is actually thinking about — delusions, phobias, obsessions, and suicidal or homicidal ideation. Contrast: thought process.
How a patient's ideas connect to one another — assessed for flight of ideas, circumstantiality, loose associations, clang associations, neologisms. Contrast: thought content.

Part of Joiner's interpersonal theory of suicide — a painful sense of social isolation and disconnection from others. Combines with perceived burdensomeness (believing oneself to be a burden on others) and acquired capability (a diminished fear of death and pain, often from repeated exposure to painful or provocative experiences) to produce the highest suicide risk.

A gradual decrease in a drug's or substance's effect at a given dose, requiring progressively larger amounts to achieve the same effect; the pharmacologic phenomenon behind escalating substance use. Contrast: withdrawal, cross-tolerance, dependence.

The phenomenon in which tolerance to one substance (such as alcohol) confers partial tolerance to a pharmacologically related substance (such as a benzodiazepine), a principle used clinically when substituting one sedative for another during detoxification.

An interaction in which two drugs together produce an effect greater than the simple sum of their individual effects (for example, combining a benzodiazepine with alcohol); a key reason for checking drug-drug interactions before coadministering CNS depressants.
Richard Lazarus and Susan Folkman's model describing stress as an ongoing interaction between a person and their environment, filtered through the person's cognitive appraisal of the situation.

A noninvasive brain stimulation treatment for depression in which a time-varying magnetic field induces an electrical current in the cortex; the patient remains awake and alert throughout. Contrast: ECT, which requires anesthesia and induces a seizure.

The patient's unconscious redirection of feelings and attitudes, originally tied to important figures from their past, onto the nurse or clinician (a new adolescent patient tells the nurse she has "the same attitude as my mother"); expected in therapeutic relationships and can be used therapeutically if recognized. Contrast: countertransference.

A Peplau-based discharge planning model in which the nurse-patient hospital relationship continues in modified form until a community-based relationship (including peer support) is established, easing the transition out of inpatient care.

A model of care that recognizes the impact of trauma on a person's life and integrates that knowledge into every policy and interaction to avoid re-traumatizing the patient; asks "what happened to you," not "what is wrong with you," and avoids re-traumatizing practices such as unnecessary restraint or locked doors.

An unexpected, unusual, often catastrophic event — natural disaster, violent crime, war, mass violence — that affects one person or many people simultaneously. Contrast: developmental crisis and situational crisis.

An amino acid found in aged, fermented, or cured foods (aged cheese, cured meats, draft beer, fava beans, soy sauce) that, when a patient is taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), cannot be broken down normally and can trigger a life-threatening hypertensive crisis.

A competitive, time-urgent, achievement-driven personality style associated with higher cardiovascular stress reactivity. Contrast: Type B (relaxed, easygoing), Type C (conflict-avoidant, responds to stress with hopelessness), Type D (distressed, pessimistic, socially inhibited).
A defense mechanism in which a symbolic act is performed to cancel out, or atone for, an unacceptable thought or action (a man with fantasies about his wife's sister takes his wife on a trip).
One of Yalom's 11 group therapy curative factors — the relief and decreased anxiety a person feels on discovering that others share the same problem ("I thought I was the only one").

Explicitly checking one's own perception of a patient's meaning against the patient's actual experience, typically using "I" statements ("I notice… I wonder if…"); overlaps with the therapeutic technique of seeking clarification.

The second most common cause of dementia, caused by multiple small strokes (infarcts) that damage brain tissue over time, producing a characteristic step-like pattern of decline rather than the smooth, gradual decline of Alzheimer disease.
The ethical duty to tell the truth, delivered with compassion — for example, giving honest answers about a diagnosis and the effects of medication.

Spoken words together with their emotional tone, context, and connotation; the sender encodes a message and the receiver decodes it, and communication is always a two-way process. Contrast: nonverbal communication, which takes priority when the two conflict.
The purposeless, repetitive utterance of words or phrases with no apparent communicative intent; seen in catatonia and chronic schizophrenia.
Extreme aggression that uses strong physical force or a weapon with the intent to inflict serious bodily harm. Contrast: aggression, a broader category that includes verbal as well as physical acts.

A therapeutic communication technique that gently questions an unlikely or distorted belief ("Really?" "From what you've told me, that doesn't sound like her") without directly arguing with it; used only when the nurse is confident of the actual facts.

A patient's self-initiated application for psychiatric treatment; the patient retains all civil rights and can leave the facility, even against medical advice, though some states allow a brief hold to evaluate the patient for involuntary status before discharge. Contrast: involuntary commitment.
A catatonic symptom in which a patient's limb or posture can be moved into a position by another person and then remains fixed there for an unusually long time.

Good physical and mental health that goes beyond the mere absence of disease, spanning eight dimensions — emotional, financial, social, spiritual, occupational, physical, intellectual, and environmental.

An acute, thiamine-deficiency brain disorder, usually from chronic alcohol use, presenting with visual disturbance, ataxia, hypotension, and confusion progressing to coma if untreated; treated emergently with IV/IM thiamine. If untreated, it can progress to the chronic Korsakoff amnestic syndrome.

A 36-item self- or proxy-reported measure of functional impairment across six domains (cognition, mobility, self-care, getting along with others, life activities, participation); DSM-5's suggested replacement for the discontinued Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF). See Global Assessment of Functioning.
A substance-specific physical and psychological syndrome that develops after the cessation or reduction of a substance to which the body has adapted. See Tolerance, Cross-tolerance.
Words strung together in a sentence with no logical connection or meaning; the most severe form of disorganized speech, seen in schizophrenia.

The middle phase of the nurse-patient relationship in which the patient identifies and actively works on problems and tries out new coping behaviors; transference and countertransference are most prominent during this phase. See Peplau's phases.

Dry mouth, common in older adults and frequently worsened by anticholinergic medications (including many antipsychotics and tricyclic antidepressants); contributes to dental decay and difficulty swallowing.

Irvin Yalom's 11 primary factors through which therapeutic change occurs in group psychotherapy, centered on the idea that a group functions as a "social microcosm" providing a corrective emotional experience: instillation of hope, universality, imparting information, altruism, corrective recapitulation of the primary family group, development of socializing techniques, imitative behavior, interpersonal learning, group cohesiveness, catharsis, and existential factors. See the individual factors alphabetized at their own letters (Altruism, Catharsis, Existential factors, Group cohesiveness, Universality) plus Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group, Development of socializing techniques, Imitative behavior, Imparting information, Instillation of hope, and Interpersonal learning below.

terms.term: Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group
names: Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group
terms.html: A Yalom curative factor in which group members relive and work through early family conflicts within the safety of the group.
A Yalom curative factor describing the basic social skills a member learns through group participation and feedback.
A Yalom curative factor in which a member adopts behaviors modeled by the therapist or by another member who has mastered a skill, such as copying a more assertive member's phrasing.
A Yalom curative factor describing the didactic instruction a group provides about mental illness, medications, development, or the treatment setting.
A Yalom curative factor in which seeing other group members make progress gives a struggling member hope, which itself helps keep patients engaged in therapy.
A Yalom curative factor combining insight, working through transference, and a corrective emotional experience as a member tests new ways of relating to others within the safety of the group.

External "time givers" — most importantly light, acting through the suprachiasmatic nucleus — that set and reset the body's internal biologic (circadian) rhythms; disruption of zeitgebers is linked to mood episodes in bipolar disorder.
